## Prep work
Today's data comes from [The Changing Childhood Project](https://changingchildhood.unicef.org/){target="_blank"} (conducted by UNICEF).  The New York Times published an intresting [article](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/17/upshot/global-survey-optimism.html){target="_blank"} based on this dataset.

- Survey data with around 1000 respondents *per country* from 21 countries
- Two age cohorts: young (15-24) vs old (40 or older)
- Most variables are Likert Scale; naming is not very intuitive (see [codebook](../../../../dataset/unicef-changing-childhood-codebook.pdf){download="unicef-changing-childhood-codebook.pdf"})

##     
```{r}
#| echo: true
library(tidyverse)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 5,
  fig.height = 3,
  out.width = "75%"
)
df.child <- read_csv("../../../../dataset/unicef-changing-childhood-data.csv")

# create a smaller dataset for simplicity
df.child.small <- df.child %>%
  filter(COUNTRYNEW %in% c("United States", "Japan", "Nigeria")) %>%
  select(COUNTRYNEW, AGE, WP22110, WP22109, WP30, WP22091)
```

- `COUNTRYNEW`: respondent's country.
- `AGE`: respondent's age group (the survey compares ages 15-24 with ages 40 and older).
- `WP22110`: minimum acceptable age for men to get married. `97` means 97 or older; `98` is "Don't know"; `99` is "Refused".
- `WP22109`: minimum acceptable age for women to get married. `97` means 97 or older; `98` is "Don't know"; `99` is "Refused".
- `WP30`: satisfaction with standard of living: `1` = satisfied, `2` = dissatisfied, `3` = "Don't know", `4` = refused.
- `WP22091`: which group the respondent most identifies with: `1` = city or area where they live, `2` = their country, `3` = the world, `8` = "Don't know", `9` = refused.



# Base R plots

## Boxplot
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 3
boxplot(df.child.small$WP22110,
  ylab = "Minimum acceptable age for men")
```


## Stem and leaf plot

- Different software often produce stem-and-leaf plots that look differently
- In R, can change *scale* and *width* arguments
- Only sometimes useful

```{r}
stem(df.child.small$WP22110)
```

## Histogram

- In base R, visualization elements can be modified by adding arguments within the function

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 4
hist(df.child.small$WP22110,
  nclass=30,
  main='Minimum acceptable age for men',
    col='lightblue', 
     ylab=NA, 
     yaxt='n',
    xlab=NA)
```


## Side-by-side boxplots
```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6
boxplot(df.child.small$WP22110 ~ df.child.small$COUNTRYNEW,
  col='salmon',
        border='darkblue',
  xlab='Country',
  ylab='Minimum acceptable age for men')
```


## Scatterplot

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 4
plot(df.child.small$WP22110, df.child.small$WP22109,
  col = as.factor(df.child.small$COUNTRYNEW),
    xlab = "Minimum acceptable age for men",
    ylab = "Minimum acceptable age for women")

abline(a=0,b=1)
```


Comment: with base R, plotting can be fast, but it's not very easy to incooperate other steps (like removing invalid values 97, 98, 99). Adding layers (e.g., a reference line) is also not very convenient.


# ggplot

## Introduction

- **ggplot2** is an alternative framework for creating plots and graphics; the package is loaded as part of **tidyverse** 

| Feature | ggplot2 | Base R plot functions |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | Unified, intuitive syntax (the "grammar of graphics") | Syntax depends on the plot type, such as `plot()` or `hist()` |
| Storing plots | Plots can be stored as ggplot objects | Plots are drawn directly rather than stored as R objects |
| Adding layers | Add layers to an existing plot with `+` | Add to the current plot with additional plotting commands |

## Example 1

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: 60%
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97, WP22109 < 97) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=WP22110, y=WP22109, color=COUNTRYNEW)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x="Minimum acceptable age for men", y="Minimum acceptable age for women", color="Country")
```

## Example 2

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: 60%
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97, WP22109 < 97) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = COUNTRYNEW, y = WP22110)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x="Country", y="Minimum acceptable age for men")
```

## Basic ingredients of a ggplot

1. Data
    - **Data frame** containing all the raw observations
    
2. Aesthetic mapping
    - An aesthetic is a visual property of the plot, such as x-axis, y-axis, color, size, etc.
    - Use **aes** to specify which **variable** is mapped to which **aesthetic**
    - Example: minimum acceptable age for men -> x-axis; minimum acceptable age for women -> y-axis; country -> color
    
3. Geoms
    - What **types** of layers should be added to the plots


## Example 1 explained

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2

ggplot(
  data=subset(df.child.small, WP22110 < 97 & WP22109 < 97), # data
  mapping=aes(
    x=WP22110, # minimum acceptable age for men maps to the x-axis
    y=WP22109, # minimum acceptable age for women maps to the y-axis
    color=COUNTRYNEW)) + # country maps to color
  geom_point() # add a scatterplot geom
```

## Example 2 explained

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
ggplot(data=subset(df.child.small, WP22110 < 97), # data
    mapping=aes(x=COUNTRYNEW, # country maps to the x-axis
      y=WP22110)) + # minimum acceptable age for men maps to the y-axis
  geom_boxplot() # add a boxplot geom
```


# geom examples

## Geom's from the first two examples

- Example 1: **geom\_point** draws scatterplot-type points for each observation
- Example 2: **geom\_boxplot** draws boxplots


## geom_violin

Use the same code for example 2, but change **geom\_boxplot** to **geom\_violin**.
```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97, WP22109 < 97) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = COUNTRYNEW, y = WP22110)) +
  geom_violin() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x="Country", y="Minimum acceptable age for men")
```


## geom_histogram
- Recall: histogram is univariate; y-axis is always frequency, so we don't need a **y=\_** mapping

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = WP22110)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(x="Minimum acceptable age for men")
```



## 
- Add arguments in geoms
```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = WP22110)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=5, fill="grey", color="blue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x="Minimum acceptable age for men")
```

- Note the differences in the syntax convention:
  + base R **col** vs ggplot **fill**
  + base R **border** vs ggplot **color**
  + esp. "color" (ggplot) vs "col" (base R)
  
  
  
##
- Add another dimension (i.e., map another variable to another aesthetic)

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = WP22110, fill=COUNTRYNEW)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=5, color="blue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x="Minimum acceptable age for men", fill="Country")
```



## geom_bar
```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP30 < 3) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=COUNTRYNEW, fill=as.factor(WP30))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x="Country", fill="Standard of living\n1 = satisfied, 2 = dissatisfied")
```


## geom_jitter
Scatterplots can be hard to read when both variables are categorical. Jitter separates overlapping responses.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP30 < 3) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=COUNTRYNEW, y=WP30, color=COUNTRYNEW)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x="Country", y="Standard of living")
```

##
Change **geom_point()** to **geom_jitter()**

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP30 < 3) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=COUNTRYNEW, y=WP30, color=COUNTRYNEW)) +
  geom_jitter() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x="Country", y="Standard of living")
```


## geom_text
```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97, WP22109 < 97) %>%
  group_by(COUNTRYNEW) %>%
  summarise(mean_male_age=mean(WP22110), 
            mean_female_age=mean(WP22109),
            .groups="drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=mean_female_age, y=mean_male_age, label=COUNTRYNEW)) +
  geom_text() +
  labs(x="mean min age for women", y="mean min age for men")
```

- Try: change **geom_text** to **geom_label**
- Try: add **geom_point**

Comment: it is very easy to combine data manipulation steps with ggplot.




# Layering and Customization to ggplot

## Customize ggplot with + 
ggplot offers a very convenient syntax (+) to add elements and layers

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97, WP22109 < 97) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=WP22110, y=WP22109, color=WP22110)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle('Marriage-age views by country') +
  labs(x='Minimum acceptable age for men', y='Minimum acceptable age for women', color='Minimum acceptable age for men')
```

## Example: change gradient color
```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97, WP22109 < 97) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=WP22110, y=WP22109, color=WP22110)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle('Marriage-age views by country') +
  labs(x='Minimum acceptable age for men', y='Minimum acceptable age for women', color='Minimum acceptable age for men') +
  scale_color_gradient(low="lightblue",high="orange") 
```



## Example: change categorical color

```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP30 < 3) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=COUNTRYNEW, fill=as.factor(WP30))) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("1"='seagreen3',"2"='tomato')) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x="Country", fill="Standard of living\n1 = satisfied, 2 = dissatisfied")
```


## Example: add a line
```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2
df.child.small %>%
  filter(WP22110 < 97, WP22109 < 97) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=WP22110, y=WP22109, color=COUNTRYNEW)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0, linetype='dashed') +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x="Minimum acceptable age for men", y="Minimum acceptable age for women", color="Country")
```


## There's more!
- There are many other geoms and customizations available!
- Each geom has its own set of aesthetics to which variables can be mapped.
- Bring up the help page to check what aesthetics are needed.
- Many references can be found online: they all share the same, unified structure that you can now understand.


## Example

`WP22091` records whether respondents identify most with their city or area (`1`), their country (`2`), or the world (`3`). `WP30` records satisfaction with standard of living: satisfied (`1`) or dissatisfied (`2`).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
df.child %>%
  filter(COUNTRYNEW %in% c("Germany", "United States"),
         WP22091 %in% 1:3, WP30 %in% 1:2) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(WP22091), y = as.factor(WP30))) +
  geom_jitter() +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~COUNTRYNEW) +
  ggtitle("Identity and standard-of-living satisfaction") +
  labs(
    x = "Identity (1 = city/area, 2 = country, 3 = world)",
    y = "Standard of living (1 = satisfied, 2 = dissatisfied)"
  )
```



# Interactive plots

## Interactive plots
- Wide variety, very flexible; can generate quite complicated graphs (for example, see [HTML widgets](http://www.htmlwidgets.org/showcase_leaflet.html))
- Many new packages and functions are being published (esp. on github)
- Currently, no "go-to" package, no unified approach
- We'll try a few simple examples to give you an idea, mostly using the [plotly](https://plot.ly/r/) package

```{r}
#| message: false
#install.packages('plotly')
library(plotly)
```


## Example 1: Histogram
- Note the difference in syntax convention (e.g.: <font color='red'> ~ </font>varname)
```{r}
#| message: false
plot_ly(data=filter(df.child.small, WP22110 < 97),
        x=~WP22110, type='histogram') %>%
  layout(xaxis=list(title="Minimum acceptable age for men"))
```

## Example 2: Boxplot
```{r}
#| message: false
plot_ly(data=filter(df.child.small, WP22110 < 97),
    y=~WP22110, x=~COUNTRYNEW, type='box') %>%
  layout(xaxis=list(title="Country"),
    yaxis=list(title="Minimum acceptable age for men"))
```




## Example 3: 2D scatterplot
```{r}
#| message: false
plot_ly(data=filter(df.child.small, WP22110 < 97, WP22109 < 97),
  x=~WP22110, y=~WP22109,
  color=~COUNTRYNEW, text=~COUNTRYNEW) %>%
  layout(xaxis=list(title="Minimum acceptable age for men"),
   yaxis=list(title="Minimum acceptable age for women"))
```



## Example 4: 3D scatterplot
```{r}
#| message: false
#| out-width: 90%
plot_ly(data=filter(df.child.small, WP22110 < 97, WP22109 < 97, WP22091 < 4),
  x=~WP22110, y=~WP22109,
  z=~WP22091, text=~COUNTRYNEW,
  color=~COUNTRYNEW, size=I(4)) %>%
    layout(scene=list(xaxis=list(title="Minimum acceptable age for men"),
      yaxis=list(title="Minimum acceptable age for women"),
        zaxis=list(title="Identity (1-3)")))
```


## Example 5: integration with ggplot
- plotly offers an easy way to make a ggplot interactive
```{r}
#| message: false
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 5
#| out-width: 80%

p1 <- df.child %>%
  filter(COUNTRYNEW %in% c("Germany", "United States"),
         WP22091 %in% 1:3, WP30 %in% 1:2) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(WP22091), y = as.factor(WP30))) +
  geom_jitter() +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~COUNTRYNEW) +
  ggtitle("Identity and standard-of-living satisfaction") +
  labs(
    x = "Identity (1 = city/area, 2 = country, 3 = world)",
    y = "Standard of living (1 = satisfied, 2 = dissatisfied)"
  )
ggplotly(p1)
```


## Exercise

- `WP22071`: whether digital technology helps children with education.
- `WP22072`: whether digital technology helps children have fun.
- For both questions, `1` = a lot, `2` = a little, and `3` = not at all. Other response codes are excluded.

Try to reproduce the following graph.  You can also use other variables of your interest (refer to the codebook).  

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
df.child %>%
  filter(WP22071 %in% 1:3, WP22072 %in% 1:3) %>%
  group_by(COUNTRYNEW) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_education = mean(WP22071),
    mean_fun = mean(WP22072),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_education, y = mean_fun, label = COUNTRYNEW)) +
  geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0, linetype="dashed") +
  geom_label() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Average views on digital technology by country",
    x = "Not helpful with education",
    y = "Not helpful with fun"
  )
```
